issues.legal_issue: A court decree that recognizes a pre-existing property right arising from a family arrangement and does not itself create that right is admissible without registration when relied on to establish title in a later pre-emption suit.
material_facts: In an earlier property suit, the claimant and a relative asserted that a family arrangement had already transferred a co-owner’s share to them.
The defendant in that suit admitted the arrangement in a written pleading and in evidence, and the court decreed the claim on that admission.
The decree recognized the asserted pre-existing right in property that was the subject matter of the earlier suit; it did not itself create a new right.
The claimant later relied on the decree to establish co-ownership and seek pre-emption against an assignee of another co-owner’s share.
The decree was not challenged as fraudulent, collusive, or made by a court lacking jurisdiction, and no gift was alleged.
issues.conclusion: The decree was admissible without registration to establish the claimant’s recognized co-ownership, and the challenge to the claimant’s right of pre-emption failed.
issues.legal_principle: Registration Act, 1908, Section 17(2)(vi), excludes court decrees and orders from compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(b) and (c), including a compromise decree confined to the suit property. A decree that merely recognizes a pre-existing right does not create a right for the first time. Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major was distinguishable because the decree there created a right for the first time; S. Noordeen v. V.S. Thiru Venkita Reddiar was consistent with distinguishing cases involving a pre-existing right. The Court also relied on the principle that a bona fide family arrangement does not require registration.

rule.if: later_preemption_suit and earlier_property_suit_decree_relied_on and claim_based_on_preexisting_family_arrangement and opposing_party_admitted_arrangement and decree_only_recognized_existing_claim and property_within_earlier_suit and not gift_alleged

predicates.later_preemption_suit: A claimant brings a suit to enforce pre-emption against an assignee of a co-owner’s share.
predicates.earlier_property_suit_decree_relied_on: A party relies on a decree from an earlier suit concerning the property to establish title in the later suit.
predicates.claim_based_on_preexisting_family_arrang: The claimant in the earlier suit asserted that a family arrangement had already given them an interest in the property before the decree.
predicates.opposing_party_admitted_arrangement: The opposing party in the earlier suit admitted the asserted arrangement in a pleading and in evidence.
predicates.decree_only_recognized_existing_claim: The earlier court granted the claim on the admission and recognized the asserted right rather than creating a new right by the decree.
predicates.property_within_earlier_suit: The property in which the right was recognized was the subject matter of the earlier suit.
predicates.gift_alleged: A party alleged that the transfer of the property was a gift.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a later pre-emption suit relies on a decree that records an admitted, pre-existing family-arrangement right in property covered by the earlier suit, and no gift is alleged, the decree may be used without registration to establish that title.

issues.legal_issue: A court decree or order is exempt from registration under the provisions governing instruments that create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish property rights, subject to the exception for a compromise decree that includes property outside the suit.
material_facts: The earlier decree was based on an admission, not a compromise decree.
The decree concerned property that was the subject matter of the earlier suit.
The asserted right arose from an earlier family arrangement, and no gift, lease, or transfer of a court decree or order was alleged.
issues.conclusion: A decree or order, including a compromise decree confined to the property that is the subject matter of the suit, does not require registration under the provisions addressing instruments that create or declare property rights; a compromise decree including property outside the suit falls within the exception.
issues.legal_principle: Registration Act, 1908, Section 17(1)(b) and (c), read with Section 17(2)(vi), exempts court decrees and orders from registration on the basis that they create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish property rights. The exception applies where a compromise decree includes immovable property outside the subject matter of the suit. The exemption does not extend to the separate categories in Section 17(1)(a), (d), and (e), including instruments effecting a gift or qualifying lease, or a transfer of a court decree or order. The Court discussed the legislative history and relied on Rani Hemanta Kumari Debi v. Midnapur Zamindari Company Limited and Mangan Lal Deoshi v. Mohammad Moinul Haque.

rule.if: court_decree_or_order and not qualifying_gift_lease_or_decree_transfer and (not compromise_decree or not compromise_includes_outside_suit_property)

predicates.court_decree_or_order: The instrument relied on is a decree or order made by a court.
predicates.qualifying_gift_lease_or_decree_transfer: The decree or order effects a gift, a qualifying lease, or a transfer of a decree or order that creates or alters rights in immovable property.
predicates.compromise_decree: The court decree records a compromise between the parties.
predicates.compromise_includes_outside_suit_propert: The compromise decree includes immovable property that was not the subject matter of the suit or proceeding.

issues.definition: A court decree or order outside the specified gift, lease, and decree-transfer categories does not require registration on this basis unless it is a compromise decree that includes property beyond the suit.

issues.legal_issue: A party may not reopen the cause of action resolved by an operative decree merely to challenge the underlying claim for want of registration.
material_facts: The earlier court had granted relief on the claimant’s asserted title and recognized the family arrangement.
The decree was relied on in the later suit, and no challenge was made that it was fraudulent, collusive, or passed without jurisdiction.
The opposing party sought to exclude the decree from consideration on the ground that the underlying right required registration.
issues.conclusion: The underlying cause of action could not be revived to examine an alleged registration defect after it had resulted in an operative decree; the decree could not be ignored on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The cause of action merges in the decree and cannot be resuscitated after adjudication. A decree is binding unless it is successfully challenged on a ground such as want of jurisdiction, fraud, or collusion; the Court referred to Section 44 of the Evidence Act and the principle stated in Spencer-Bower and Turner on Res Judicata.

rule.if: later_proceeding_relies_on_prior_decree and prior_claim_adjudicated_into_decree and registration_defect_used_to_reopen_underlying_claim and not decree_challenged_for_fraud_collusion_or_lack_of_jurisdiction

predicates.later_proceeding_relies_on_prior_decree: A party relies on an earlier court decree in a later proceeding.
predicates.prior_claim_adjudicated_into_decree: The claim concerning the right was presented to a court and resolved by a decree.
predicates.registration_defect_used_to_reopen_under: A party seeks to revisit the underlying claim on the ground that the transaction or right required registration.
predicates.decree_challenged_for_fraud_collusion_or: A party challenges the decree on the ground that it was fraudulent, collusive, or made without jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When an earlier decree resolved the claim, a party relying on it in a later proceeding cannot reopen the underlying claim solely for a registration defect if the decree is not challenged on the stated grounds.
